items.summary: When the floodwaters rose around their home in Rajapul on July 19, Bandana Buragohain had no way of getting out on her own. The 70-year-old clung to the back of a man from her village as he waded into the current. At one point, the force of the water pushed him backwards. A couple of other boys came and helped carry her to a nearby house with a terrace, where around 30 others had already taken shelter. “I somehow managed to stay alive. I could have died,” she recalled. Rajapul, in the Nazira subdivision of Sivasagar district, was among the areas caught in the path of what several reports have described as one of Assam's worst localised floods since the 1950s. After days of heavy rain across the region, including 137 mm recorded over eight to nine hours in the neighbouring hills of Nagaland , a sudden rush of water moved downstream into the plains on July 19, sending the Dikhow, Disang and Janji, rivers that eventually meet the Brahmaputra, above extreme flood levels within hours and engulfing settlements before families could evacuate. The same rainfall triggered multiple landslides in Nagaland’s Mon district, killing nine people. The death toll climbed to 100, with more than 2.12 lakh people affected across Sivasagar, Charaideo, Jorhat and Golaghat districts. Livestock losses were extensive, and 17,198 hectares of agricultural land were submerged. Within Sivasagar district, Nepali Khuti in Bihubar emerged as the epicentre of the disaster, with more than 300 families left destitute. Videos from the village showed bodies being recovered from beneath layers of silt. Weeks on, the water has drained out of most of Sivasagar, but little else has been restored. For families in the affected villages, the livestock is gone, the sowing window has passed, and many still wait for cash assistance. A Delhi High Court bench has done what a Delhi civic agency thought was long overdue: turned down an order that could have drained crores in public money while letting a luxury hotel chain sit on prime Lutyens’ Delhi land for a fraction of what it’s worth. items.title: Arbitrating a class action?
items.summary: On June 8, 2026, the Supreme Court closed the doors on India's most significant shareholder class action in 3 paragraphs of consent. It referred the dispute to arbitration, quashed 2 rulings by the company law tribunal and overlooked a crucial underlying question: can a class action representing 40,000 (approx) shareholders be an arbitrable subject matter, brought on behalf of all by anyone at a roll of dice? The Jindal Poly Films Ltd v. Monet Securities Pvt Ltd was not an in personam dispute but an in rem dispute. It was filed under Section 245 of the Companies Act, 2013 as a representative suit on behalf of 40,000 (approx) shareholders; sleeping since its inception into the statute until this filing brought it to life. The same life has now ended by consent, not by reasoning. What the Court did The suit was brought by shareholders holding under 5% of Jindal Poly Films. They averred acquisition of preference shares in a subsidiary by promoter-linked entities at below fair market value for about ₹105 crore as against a higher fair value. Loans were written off, stakes in another subsidiary were also sold away at below fair market value and loss estimated by an independent valuer put above ₹2,500 crore. This was engineered to circumvent the threshold requirements which mandate minority shareholder approval. The tribunal's order totalled 61 pages and remains the most developed reading Section 245 has received. It held that Section 245 protects the company (the entity) in addition to protecting its members; reaches transactions already concluded, through the compensation remedy built into the section; and should not be limited by a borrowed US test designed for a different kind of shareholder claim. The appellate tribunal seconded this through 29 more pages of reasoning. As part of this process, notice to the entire class had already been ordered. items.title: Can Right to Education Act apply to madrasas, vedic pathshalas? Supreme Court to examine
items.summary: The Supreme Court on Wednesday agreed to consider a plea challenging provisions of the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009 (RTE Act) concerning minority schools, madrasas, vedic pathshalas and institutions primarily imparting religious instruction. [Pyare Ziya Khan v. UOI] A Bench of Justices Dipankar Datta and Sheel Nagu directed that the public interest litigation (PIL) filed by Maharashtra State Minority Commission Chairman Pyare Zia Khan be heard with a pending case concerning the application of the RTE Act and the Teacher Eligibility Test (TET) to minority educational institutions. In that case, the Supreme Court questioned its 2014 ruling exempting minority schools from the ambit of the RTE Act and sought consideration of the issue by a larger bench. Justices Dipankar Datta and Sheel Nagu Khan has challenged Sections 1(4) and 1(5) of the RTE Act as violative of Articles 14, 15, 21 and 21A of the Constitution. Section 1(4) provides that the RTE Act will apply subject to Articles 29 and 30, which protect the cultural and educational rights of minorities. Section 1(5) states that the Act will not apply to madrasas, vedic pathshalas and educational institutions primarily imparting religious instruction. The petition has also sought a declaration that the TET, introduced under the RTE Act and notifications issued by the National Council for Teacher Education (NCTE), is mandatory for teachers in all schools covered by Section 2(n) of the Act. It argued that the provisions create separate classes of children based solely on the character of the institution in which they study. This classification has no rational connection with the RTE Act’s object of ensuring universal and quality elementary education, the plea contended. It added that the phrase “primarily imparting religious instruction” has not been defined. According to the plea, the law provides no criteria, threshold or designated authority for deciding whether an institution falls within this exemption. Khan maintained that prescribing minimum qualifications for teachers would not interfere with the right of minorities to establish and administer educational institutions. Such institutions would remain free to select and appoint teachers from among candidates who satisfy the prescribed standards, he argued. items.title: BCI grants one-time enrolment relief to law grads given permission to write exams despite attendance shortage
items.summary: The Bar Council of India (BCI) has ruled that law graduates who were permitted by the Supreme Court to appear for examinations despite attendance shortage as a one-time exception cannot be denied enrolment as advocates. In a communication dated August 12, Justice Rajendra Menon , Co-Chairperson of the BCI's Legal Education Committee, said that the attendance deficiency excused for the purpose of exams cannot be revived at the enrolment stage. " The one-time protection cannot reasonably be divided into two inconsistent stages whereby the attendance shortage is disregarded for lawful completion of the recognised professional degree but is revived immediately thereafter as the sole ground for denying consideration for entry into the profession," the order stated. The issue arose following the Delhi High Court's judgment delivered in proceedings initiated upon the death by suicide of a law student in Amity University. The BCI subsequently directed institutions not to bar students from examinations solely for attendance shortage during the relevant period. In May this year, the Supreme Court stayed the High Court's judgment on an appeal by the BCI. Thereafter, in July, the apex court granted one-time protection to students whose academic session was underway when the High Court verdict was passed, permitting them to sit for final or supplementary examinations despite the shortfall. The representations that prompted the order came from Faculty of Law, Delhi University students, who said that they had lawfully completed their degrees under the Supreme Court's protection but could not secure enrolment because their universities did not issue the standard attendance certificate. To resolve this, the BCI has permitted universities and Centres of Legal Education (CLEs) to issue an alternative certificate confirming that a candidate who falls within the protected class and passes the examination and obtains a degree is eligible for enrolment. The order specifies that historical attendance records cannot be altered or deemed regular. The arrangement applies uniformly to all similarly placed candidates across India and is not confined to Delhi University. items.title: The liminal award: 'Fluid entitlement' and the decoupling of interim protection post-award
items.summary: Indian arbitration, for decades, treated the issuance of an award as an event of absolute closure; until then the disputants were parties, and after the award Indian law divided them into 'award-holder' and 'judgment-debtor'. The High Court of Bombay in Dirk India made this into a doctrine, holding that post-award interim protection under Section 9 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 exists only to ensure the 'fruits of the award' to the award holder, and the unsuccessful party has nothing to protect because it lost everything. Hence Section 9 was barred to it; only Section 36's conditional protection remained. In Home Care Retail Marts Pvt. Ltd. v. Haresh N. Sanghavi , the Supreme Court rejects the binary: the losing party may seek interim protection under Section 9 even after the award, decoupling that protection from the question of winning or losing. This is what I call 'fluid entitlement', since an award can be severable, modifiable and/or set aside, and a full set aside can lead to further arbitration; the unsuccessful party, accordingly, remains a substantive entity with a suspended future claim. Move I: The liminal space: Decoupling the fruits from the subject matter The move at the heart of Home Care Retail Marts is a new reading of what Section 9 protects. According to Dirk India , Section 9 aids enforcement and nothing else; Justice Manmohan demolishes that principle by asking not whether the party has won but whether the subject matter is vulnerable. Section 9 protects 'the subject matter of arbitration' and 'the amount in dispute', language much broader than the limited fiction of 'fruits'. While a Section 34 application is pending, the award stands as an intermediate stage and not a final event, so the unsuccessful party is entitled to protect the subject matter for this period, lest the award is quashed and the following arbitration has nothing to arbitrate. Move II: Structural bypass: Friction between Section 9 and Section 36(3) Fluid entitlement solves one asymmetry but creates another. Section 36(3) is rigorous in nature; Section 9 provides the far more flexible standard of what 'appears to the court to be "just and convenient."' This creates a tactical escape hatch, as a losing party can claim almost anything as a "non-prejudicial" measure or maintain the status quo in the name of preserving assets. items.summary: The Central government told the Supreme Court on Thursday that it has agreed in principle to formulate a policy granting railway travel concessions to acid attack survivors, particularly to help them travel for medical treatment. A Bench of Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant , Justice Joymalya Bagchi and Justice V Mohana was hearing a plea by Atijeevan Society seeking railway concessions and reservation benefits for acid attack survivors. CJI Kant pointed out that acid attack survivors are already recognised as persons with disabilities under the law. He noted that the issue could be addressed as part of a social welfare measure. "Putting them in the disabled category, that has now been statutorily resolved, with the amendment through another petition before us," he said. Chief Justice of India Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana Additional Solicitor General Archana Pathak Dave submitted that the Centre is proposing to extend the concession under the existing “patient category”, rather than create a separate concession under the disability category. Dave said the government has reservations about granting the benefit under the disability category as it could lead to demands from other categories of persons with disabilities for similar concessions. However, she said the Centre was willing to provide the concession because acid attack survivors require travel for medical treatment. items.title: Bowing to corporate pressure? Supreme Court slams FSSAI's reluctance to put warning labels on foods high in sugar, salt, fat
items.summary: The Supreme Court on Thursday questioned the reluctance of the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) to introduce front-of-pack warning labels on packaged food products containing high levels of sugar, salt and saturated fat. A Bench of Justices JB Pardiwala and KV Viswanathan was hearing a case in which the Court had earlier urged the FSSAI to consider introducing such warning labels in the interest of public health. Today, the Court took critical note that the FSSAI was hesitant to implement such a measure, going by a the minutes of a meeting held by the food standards watchdog. The Court asked if the FSSAI was bowing down to corporate entities involved in food manufacture. " Are you taking the court for a toss? ... There is immense pressure at the end of all these corporate houses on you. And you are succumbing to that pressure! We are doing this in public interest. Keep it in mind. We are not doing it for ourselves. Why are you not abiding by our order? What have you done so far? We know the pressure on you. Will you do it on your own or should we pass an order?" the Bench remarked. The Court was also not impressed by an explanation that many Indian foods, like namkeens, would also end up being labelled as high in fat, sugar or salt if such warning labels are introduced. " You don’t want people of this country to remain healthy? More particularly growing children? " the Court asked. items.title: Kerala High Court grants bail to four more CPI(M) workers booked for attacking ED officials
items.summary: The Kerala High Court on Tuesday granted bail to four CPI(M) workers booked for allegedly attacking Enforcement Directorate (ED) officials who were returning after a search operation conducted at the residence of the former Kerala Chief Minister Pinarayi Vijayan. Justice Kauser Edappagath allowed the bail applications filed by accused Lenin Raj, Amal SP, Vaisakh and Rahul A. Justice Kauser Edappagath The development comes a day after the Court granted bail to nine other accused persons in the same case. The matter concerns an incident from May 27. ED officials had conducted a search at former CM and CPI(M) leader Pinarayi Vijayan's residence, where Vijayan and his daughter, Veena Thaikkandiyil resided. The search was part of the central agency's investigation into the CMRL case involving allegations against Exalogic, the IT company owned by Thaikkandiyil. After the search, a crowd of around 300 persons are said to have surrounded the ED officials' convoy and attacked the vehicles with stones, bricks, sticks and iron rods causing damage. Subsequently, the Museum Police registered a case invoking various provisions of the Bhartiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), including Section 109 (attempt to murder), along with Section 3 (1) of the Prevention of Damage to Public Property Act. 14 accused persons who were arrested in the matter have now secured bail. One, Harishkumar was the first to get bail from a trial court. The State has challenged this trial court order before the High Court and sought the cancellation of Harishkumar's bail. This appeal remains pending. Yesterday, the Court granted bail to nine other accused, observing that even though the allegations were serious, they had remained in custody for over two months. The Court further noted that the investigation was almost complete and none of the bail applicants had any serious criminal antecedents. Thus, their continued detention was not required, the Court opined while granting them bail. items.title: Tamil Nadu: Nine-year-old girl allegedly sexually assaulted while walking home
items.summary: A nine-year-old Class 4 student was allegedly sexually assaulted by an unidentified man while she was walking home in Denkanikottai in Tamil Nadu’s Krishnagiri district on the evening of August 12, Wednesday. The child was walking home with three other children, but the three reached their homes before her, leaving her alone when the alleged assault took place, according to police. The incident was reported around 1 am on Thursday after the child’s mother lodged a complaint with the Denkanikottai All Women Police Station (AWPS). Police have registered an FIR under Section 87 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) (kidnapping, abducting or inducing woman to compel her marriage, etc) and Section 5(6) of the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act. The child was taken to Krishnagiri Government Hospital for a medical examination. Police said the examination will help determine whether a sexual assault took place. A police team has also visited the scene and is collecting evidence and other information as part of the investigation. The child does not know the identity of the alleged accused, but has told police that she would be able to identify him.

items.title: ‘Bid to eliminate the messenger’: Social media takedowns leaving users in the dark
items.summary: Posts by journalists, political parties, activists and media organisations are increasingly being restricted or taken down on platforms such as Meta and X, following government notices issued under Section 79(3)(b) of the Information Technology Act. This trend has raised concerns over transparency, due process and press freedom in India. The stakes are particularly high for journalists and creators who don’t have institutional backing, according to freelance journalist Sachin Gupta. “When we share hate speech or violence on social media, the government should take cognisance of those posts and take action against the people making the hate speech, rather than against those who are posting or sharing it. This is, in a way, an attempt to eliminate the messenger so that such things do not come out.” Between July and December 2025, Meta restricted over 41,000 pieces of content in India, which is nearly triple the number recorded a year earlier, according to its report on content restrictions in India. More recent figures will be published at the end of this month, according to a Meta employee Newslaundry spoke to. In light of a police drive to weed out abusive Jantar Mantar videos, there are accusations of a surge in restrictions. Sachin Gupta pointed to a lack of clarity around such restrictions and said, “Independent and freelance journalists and social media creators who do not have a platform to publish their news or information use social media to post it. If you get such posts deleted or removed, where will these people go?” X sent Sachin Gupta two takedown notices Sachin Gupta received two notices from X seeking the removal of two of his posts. One notice was from Saharanpur Police and the second was from Muzaffarnagar Police . Gupta said inspector-rank officers sent both notices. He claimed that when he contacted senior officers in both districts, they said they had no information about the inspector-level officers having issued instructions to remove his posts. One of the posts contained a video of Hindutva activist Pinki Chaudhary, in which he is seen announcing that he’ll perform a Hindu ritual at Darul Uloom Deoband, an Islamic seminary. The second video was about the recent Kanwar Yatra, in which Kanwariyas had blocked the Delhi-Haridwar highway. The Muzaffarnagar Police claimed that the video was promoting violence. items.title: Nearly a century ago, Dravidian magazines were advocating for women’s reproductive freedom
items.summary: Follow TNM's WhatsApp channel for news updates and story links. The debate over abortion in Tamil Nadu has acquired a new political and religious context after Tamil Nadu Assembly Speaker JCD Prabhakar participated in the fifth National March for Life in Chennai on August 8 and 9 and spoke against abortion. He said at the event that life begins at conception and said the issue would be brought to the attention of Chief Minister C Joseph Vijay. India’s abortion law wasn’t always about a woman’s right to choose. Under the colonial-era IPC, abortion was largely a criminal offence, but the unsafe abortions and deaths that followed led the government-appointed Shantilal Shah Committee to recommend changes. Its recommendations eventually led to the Medical Termination of Pregnancy Act in 1971, allowing abortion in specified circumstances. But nearly a century ago, the question of controlling pregnancy was being debated in the pages of Kudi Arasu and Pagutharivu , magazines associated with the Self-Respect Movement and founded by Dravidian icon Periyar. Their writings did not offer one simple position on abortion. Read together, they distinguished between preventing conception and terminating a pregnancy, while repeatedly arguing for birth control because of the consequences of repeated pregnancies for women. The discussion also went beyond population or family finances. It dealt with women's health, marriage, religion, poverty and the question of who should have control over childbearing. In an April 6, 1930, article titled ‘Karppathadai’ (contraception), Kudi Arasu described birth control as essential for “women’s liberation and self-sovereignty”. The article, likely written by Periyar, noted that others supported birth control for reasons including women's physical health, the ability to support children and the economic condition of families and the country. But it said these were not its primary concern. Its emphasis was women's freedom and independence. The article gave an example of a woman trapped in an unhappy situation because she had children to care for. According to the article, pregnancy was particularly an obstacle to women's independence and was also a major cause of women falling ill, ageing prematurely and having shorter lives.
